text.title: Contextual Inquiry Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules for contextual inquiry: the four principles recorded per session, real work in the real environment, observation kept structurally separate from interpretation, interpretations validated in the room, artifacts captured rather than described, and the cross-session floor before an observation becomes a theme.

rule.statement: Each row in `sessions` MUST record how the four principles were met: context (where the session happened and that real work was in progress), partnership (master/apprentice — participant works, researcher watches and asks, no scripted question list read start to finish), interpretation (readings shared aloud and corrected), focus (the declared research focus in force for that session).

rationale.source: Beyer & Holtzblatt, Contextual Design: Defining Customer-Centered Systems (1998), ch. 3

rule.rationale: The four principles are what separates contextual inquiry from an interview done at someone's desk. Drop partnership and the participant reverts to answering questions in summary form, which is the exact abstraction level contextual inquiry exists to get underneath.

rule.statement: A session counts as contextual inquiry only if the participant performs ongoing real work with their own data, tools and interruptions, in the place they normally do it (physical or their actual screen/session for remote work). Demonstrations from memory, conference-room walkthroughs and demo accounts MUST be labelled `retrospective` and excluded from behavioural claims in `themes`.

rationale.source: Beyer & Holtzblatt, Contextual Design — context principle

rule.rationale: The findings contextual inquiry uniquely produces are the ones the participant cannot recall to report: the second spreadsheet kept beside the app, the sticky note with the code, the field they always paste into. A demo account has none of them, so a retrospective session returns the official process rather than the practised one.

rule.statement: Every `observation_rows` entry MUST fill `action` and/or `quote` with literal, non-inferential content and keep `interpretation` in its own field. A row with an interpretation and no observed action or verbatim quote is deleted, not softened.

rationale.source: Beyer & Holtzblatt, Contextual Design — interpretation as a separable layer

rule.rationale: Once merged into one narrative sentence, no later reader can tell which half was seen and which was theorised, and the theorised half survives review because it reads like data. Requirements then get built on the researcher's model of the work rather than the work.

rule.statement: Interpretations MUST be spoken back to the participant during the session and their response recorded (confirmed / corrected / partly). Rows whose interpretation was never voiced MUST carry `validated=false` and MUST NOT be used as sole support for a theme.

rationale.source: Beyer & Holtzblatt, Contextual Design — interpretation principle

rule.rationale: Participants correct a wrong reading instantly and cheaply ("no, I only copy it out when the export is stale"), and that qualifier is unrecoverable after the session. An unvalidated reading is a hypothesis that will be promoted to a requirement by nothing more than time passing.

rule.statement: Every artifact the participant touches — spreadsheet, printed checklist, sticky note, chat thread, exported CSV, whiteboard — MUST be captured as a photo, screenshot or file reference in the row's `artifact` field, with consent and redaction noted. A prose description is not a capture.

rationale.source: Beyer & Holtzblatt, Contextual Design — artifact models

rule.rationale: Self-made artifacts encode the structure of the work: the columns of a private tracking spreadsheet are the data model the person actually needs, and the order of a hand-written checklist is the real task sequence. Described from memory, both collapse to "they keep some notes".

rule.statement: `themes` MUST cover every distinct role in the work practice, and each theme MUST cite observation rows from at least two different participants. A pattern seen in one session is recorded as a case with `n=1` stated in the theme text, never as a finding about the role.

rationale.source: Holtzblatt & Beyer, Contextual Design (2nd ed., 2017) — interviewing across roles before consolidation

rule.rationale: Individual work practice contains a large amount of personal idiosyncrasy; the shared structure only becomes visible when two people who never met do the same odd thing. Consolidating from one session propagates one person's workaround into the design as if it were the practice.

rule.statement: Skip when (a) no access to a live work setting can be obtained, or the work is legally unobservable (clinical, classified, regulated customer data) and redaction would remove the content — use diary study or interviews instead; (b) the question is about a product that does not exist yet and has no current analogue practice; (c) the question is comparative or quantitative ("which label wins", "what share of users") — contextual inquiry produces no rates; (d) the work is instantaneous and fully instrumented, where telemetry already answers the question at lower cost.
rule.rationale: Without access to real, ongoing work the method loses its only advantage over an interview while keeping its full cost in researcher hours, and the resulting report will be defended as field data despite containing none.
